strengths: Conceptual motivation: Reframing video object removal as a video-to-video stochastic bridge between the original video distribution and the clean background distribution is well-motivated, preserving structural context compared to uninformative Gaussian noise initialization.

Clear mathematical presentation: The paper clearly outlines the VP-SDE Bridge formulation, the ternary marginal interpolation, velocity-matching objective, and corresponding inference discretization algorithm.
Qualitative visual demonstration: The visual comparisons in Figures 2–4 illustrate promising visual fidelity and suggest an ability to erase auxiliary artifacts like cast shadows.
weaknesses: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation: The experimental section contains no numerical metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVD, or optical flow warping error for temporal consistency) on recognized video inpainting/removal benchmarks (such as DAVIS, YouTube-VOS, or the ROSE benchmark test split).

No ablation studies: There are no ablation experiments to validate the core technical claims. Specifically, there is no empirical evidence showing the impact of the stochastic bridge versus standard noise-to-data diffusion/flow matching baselines, nor any evaluation isolating the effect of the proposed Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM).

Simplicity and questionable mechanism of AMM: The proposed AMM in Eq. (15) is simply multiplying background patch embeddings by a global scalar $(1 + \gamma)$. The paper claims this dynamically balances generative flexibility and background fidelity across object scales, but a single global scalar does not adapt to local mask geometry or scale, and its interaction with Transformer normalization layers (e.g., LayerNorm/RMSNorm) is unanalyzed.

Subjective and limited experimental validation: Relying entirely on a few cherry-picked qualitative comparison frames without user studies, quantitative validation, or failure mode analysis does not meet the empirical standards of the venue.

strengths: Formulating video object removal as a video-to-video translation task using a stochastic bridge (VP-SDE bridge) rather than standard noise-to-data diffusion is a conceptually sound and intuitive perspective that aims to retain background context.
The theoretical framework for the VP-SDE bridge, the velocity-matching objective, and the derivation of the sampling algorithm are clearly formulated and presented.
The qualitative results presented in Figures 2–4 show visually pleasing inpainting with good handling of incidental shadows on the selected examples.
weaknesses: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation: The paper contains no quantitative benchmark results. Standard video inpainting/removal metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID/FVD, and temporal warping error / flow consistency) on standard benchmarks such as DAVIS, YouTube-VOS, or the ROSE evaluation split are entirely missing.

Lack of ablation studies: There are no ablation experiments—neither quantitative nor qualitative—to support the core claims. Crucial design choices, including the bridge formulation versus standard noise-to-data diffusion, the dual-role conditioning scheme, and the proposed Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM), are not ablated.

Under-analyzed and simplistic modulation mechanism: AMM is formulated by multiplying unmasked background patch embeddings by a single learnable scalar $(1 + \gamma)$ (Eq. 15). Without empirical analysis of what $\gamma$ learns, sensitivity studies, or comparisons against standard masking/conditioning baselines, it is impossible to assess whether this mechanism provides genuine benefit or solves the stated trade-off.

Limited experimental evaluation and baseline coverage: The experimental section spans less than one column on Page 6. Only three visual examples are showcased against three baselines (GenOmnimatte, ROSE, VACE), omitting prominent and dedicated video inpainting models cited in the related work such as DiffuEraser and ProPainter.

Incomplete manuscript details: The text points to an appendix for key mathematical derivations (e.g., on page 4: 'derived from the time-derivative of the bridge process (see Appendix)'), but no appendix or supplementary material is included.

strengths: The conceptual formulation of framing video object removal as a video-to-video translation task via a stochastic bridge (VP-SDE bridge) rather than standard noise-to-data diffusion is well-motivated and provides a sensible prior-preserving perspective.
The theoretical exposition in Sections 3 and 4 regarding VP-SDE bridge formulation and velocity matching is clearly written and logically structured.
The qualitative comparisons in Figures 2-4 show clean visual results, notably demonstrating the ability to remove collateral artifacts like shadows.
weaknesses: Complete absence of quantitative evaluation: Despite the abstract and introduction claiming that 'extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods', there are zero quantitative results in the paper. Standard video inpainting/removal metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVD, flow warping error) and user preference studies are entirely omitted.

No ablation studies: There is no experimental validation or ablation analyzing the key components of the method, such as comparing the VP-SDE bridge against standard Gaussian-noise diffusion, validating the dual-role conditioning, or evaluating the contribution of the Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM).

Misleading characterization of Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM): The paper repeatedly claims that AMM 'dynamically modulates input embeddings based on mask characteristics' (Abstract) and 'balances performance across objects of varying scales' (Contributions). However, Equation 15 shows that AMM merely scales background patch embeddings by a single learned scalar $(1 + \gamma)$. It does not dynamically adapt to mask size, shape, motion, or any spatial properties.

Extremely sparse experimental analysis: Section 5 consists of only setup details and a single qualitative comparison paragraph. The main text finishes on page 6, with figures and references taking up pages 7 to 10, leaving the empirical section severely underdeveloped for an archival conference paper.
Missing appendix/proofs: Equation 11 references an Appendix ('see Appendix') for the derivation of the velocity target $u_t$, but no appendix is provided in the submission.

strengths: Principled reformulation: Formulating video object removal as a direct stochastic bridge between the source video distribution and the clean target distribution is a well-motivated departure from standard noise-to-data video inpainting models, effectively preserving temporal and background context.

Insightful problem identification and solution: The authors identify a key limitation of bridge models in editing tasks—namely, that rigid adherence to the source prior hinders the removal of large objects—and address it with Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM) to balance fidelity and generative flexibility.

Solid theoretical foundation: Appendix B provides clear derivations for the VP-SDE bridge marginal distribution, guidance term, and the equivalence of the velocity-matching loss to denoising bridge score matching.

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: Evaluated on DAVIS and a newly proposed benchmark (BridgeRemoval-Bench) against strong contemporary baselines (e.g., ROSE, VACE, GenOmnimatte), the method demonstrates consistent improvements in background preservation metrics (PSNR, MSE, LPIPS), temporal coherence (CLIP-F), user studies, and inference efficiency (1.11 s/frame).
weaknesses: Unfinished text and presentation glitches: The manuscript contains multiple incomplete dangling sentences where URLs/links were meant to be placed (e.g., end of Abstract: 'The project page is', end of Section 5.3: 'More samples can be visited at:', and Appendix F: 'More qualitative samples can be visited at:'). While blinding is expected, leaving sentences truncated affects presentation quality.

Lack of quantitative ablation for AMM: Section 5.4 defers ablations to Appendix C, and Appendix C.1 only provides a single qualitative figure (Figure 4) demonstrating the effect of AMM on a large object. A systematic quantitative ablation (e.g., comparing performance across different mask area bins with and without AMM) is missing.

Evaluation metrics limitation: Quantitative metrics like PSNR, MSE, and LPIPS are computed exclusively on unmasked background regions because ground-truth backgrounds inside masked areas do not exist for real test sets. Consequently, the quality inside the inpainted mask is primarily judged via CLIP-T/CLIP-F and user study; reporting evaluation on a fully-supervised synthetic test set (where ground-truth removed backgrounds are available) would provide a clearer picture of inpainting fidelity.

Modest architectural novelty of AMM: The Adaptive Mask Modulation mechanism is essentially a standard FiLM-style affine transformation applied to patch tokens based on 3D convolutions over the binary mask.

strengths: Sound and well-motivated formulation: Reformulating video object removal as a video-to-video translation task via a VP-SDE stochastic bridge effectively leverages the input video as a structural prior, avoiding the need to synthesize entire scenes from scratch as in pure noise-to-data diffusion models.

Solid theoretical derivations: The paper provides clear mathematical derivations (in Section 4 and Appendix B) demonstrating the bridge marginal distribution, the tractability of the drift guidance term, and the equivalence of the velocity matching loss to bridge score matching.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluated against multiple recent baselines (e.g., ROSE, VACE, GenOmnimatte, ICVE) on both DAVIS and the newly proposed 150-video BridgeRemoval-Bench, achieving strong quantitative scores (PSNR, MSE, CLIP-T, CLIP-F) and favorable user study ratings.

Detailed algorithmic implementation: Includes comprehensive training and inference pseudo-code comparisons between standard flow matching and the proposed bridge model, clarifying practical reproducibility.
weaknesses: Lack of a strictly controlled bridge vs. flow matching ablation: While Table 3 and pseudo-code contrast BridgeRemoval with flow matching baselines, the experimental comparison does not evaluate bridge modeling vs. standard flow matching under identical training data (the 47k dataset) and backbone architecture (Wan2.1-1.3B). Existing baselines (ROSE, VACE) differ in pre-training data, multi-stage pipelines, and objectives, making it hard to isolate the exact empirical gain strictly attributable to the bridge formulation.

Missing quantitative ablation for Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM): Section C.1 evaluates AMM solely via a single visual case study (Figure 4). A comprehensive quantitative ablation across DAVIS or BridgeRemoval-Bench measuring PSNR, MSE, and CLIP-T with and without AMM (and varying object mask area ratios) is necessary to substantiate claims regarding large-scale occlusion handling.

Drafting oversights and incomplete links: Multiple sentences cut off abruptly where links/placeholders should be, including the Abstract ('The project page is'), Section 5.3 ('More samples can be visited at:'), and Section F ('More qualitative samples can be visited at:').

Clarification needed on background evaluation and post-blending: Because the bridge starts from the source latent, unmasked regions naturally stay close to the source. The authors should clarify whether the reported unmasked region metrics (PSNR/MSE/LPIPS) are measured directly on raw model output latents/decoded frames or if explicit Poisson/alpha mask blending with original input pixels was applied during post-processing.

strengths: Sound and well-motivated formulation: Reformulating video object removal as an SDE-based stochastic bridge between source and target video distributions effectively resolves the inefficiency and instability of conventional noise-to-data diffusion paradigms, preserving structural and environmental background priors.

Theoretical grounding: The manuscript provides thorough mathematical derivations in the appendix, connecting the ternary interpolation of the VP-SDE bridge to DDBM score matching and velocity prediction.

Thoughtful design of Adaptive Mask Modulation (AMM): The authors identify and address a key vulnerability of bridge models—the excessive adherence to source priors that hinders large object erasure—via a spatially adaptive FiLM-style modulation mechanism.

Solid empirical results: The method demonstrates strong performance over competitive recent baselines (such as ROSE, VACE, and GenOmnimatte) on both DAVIS and the newly proposed BridgeRemoval-Bench, supported by quantitative metrics, visual comparisons, and a user study.

Contribution of BridgeRemoval-Bench: Introducing a diverse 150-video benchmark covering real-world stock footage, synthetic videos, and challenging in-the-wild clips helps overcome the small scale and static nature of previous evaluation sets.
weaknesses: Disentanglement of data scaling vs. architectural contribution: BridgeRemoval is trained on 47k pairs (including 31k newly curated real-world composite pairs). It is not fully clear how much of the performance advantage over baselines (e.g., ROSE, which was originally trained only on 16k synthetic pairs) stems from the bridge formulation versus the larger and more dynamic training set. A direct ablation comparing standard Flow Matching vs. the Bridge framework trained on identical data would solidify the core claim.

Lack of quantitative ablation for AMM: Section C.1 only provides a single qualitative visual example (a bus occupying ~80% of the frame) to demonstrate the efficacy of Adaptive Mask Modulation. Reporting quantitative metrics (e.g., PSNR, LPIPS, CLIP-T) with and without AMM, particularly binned by mask size, would substantiate its necessity.

Incomplete sentences and missing links: The manuscript contains multiple unfinished sentences where URLs or links were omitted (e.g., Page 1: 'The project page is', Page 7: 'More samples can be visited at:', Page 17: 'More qualitative samples can be visited at:').

Minor notation inconsistencies: The text occasionally alternates between terminal index notation ($z_T$ vs. $z_1$) across Equations (7), (8), and (9)-(10), which can momentarily confuse readers regarding the continuous time interval $[0, 1]$.
